Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette: Giovanni "Gio" Bianchi still wakes up in the dead of night, his heart racing, with the same terror he felt that day in 'Nam. It's been over 40 years since the ambush that changed everything, but the memories remain as vivid as ever. Gio can't recall the exact date or time it happened, but he remembers the chaos – the sound of gunfire, the screams of his comrades, and the feeling of being completely helpless. When Gio tries to describe what happened, he's met with an unsettling silence. He knows what occurred, but the words get stuck in his throat. It's as if his mind is trying to protect him from reliving that moment. The guilt that washes over him whenever he thinks about it is crushing. Why did he make it out alive when so many others didn't? Gio can't shake off the feeling that he doesn't deserve to be here. Over time, Gio has learned to avoid certain things that remind him of that fateful day. He never goes near the Veterans' Memorial Park in his town, as the monument's design eerily resembles the terrain where the ambush took place. He also avoids wearing anything with camouflage patterns or military insignia – it's just too much for him to bear. Gio has become a master at distracting himself from intrusive thoughts about the event. When memories start creeping into his mind, he quickly shifts his focus to something else, often immersing himself in work. As a warehouse worker, Gio is always on the move, which suits him fine. He finds comfort in the routine and physical demands of the job. However, there are times when the familiar sounds of machinery or the smell of diesel fuel transport him back to that moment. When this happens, Gio's colleagues notice a change in his demeanor – he becomes withdrawn and quiet. Gio feels like a stranger in his own life. He struggles to connect with his partner, Maria, who tries her best to be supportive but can't fully understand what he's going through. Gio's sense of identity is fragmented; he no longer recognizes the man he once was. The world seems like a treacherous place, full of hidden dangers waiting to strike. Maria has been encouraging Gio to seek help for years, but it wasn't until recently that he realized he couldn't keep living in a state of constant hypervigilance. A few weeks ago, Gio had a particularly harrowing flashback while working on the warehouse floor. He became disoriented and almost got into an accident with a forklift. It was then that he knew he needed professional help to confront his demons. As Gio sits in the therapist's office, he's filled with a mix of emotions – anxiety about facing his past, hope for healing, and fear of what might surface during therapy. He's uncertain about what lies ahead but knows he can't continue living like this. For the first time in decades, Gio is willing to confront the memories he's been avoiding, even if it means reliving that fateful day all over again.
